messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Data grouping question
parts:
Maybe there's something I am not understanding here, but why not just run lm() on the raw data?

dta <- data.frame(regime=c(rep(1,10),rep(2,10),rep(3,10)))
dta$val <- c(rnorm(10, mean=8),rnorm(10, mean=4),rnorm(10, mean=2))

model <- lm(val ~ regime, dta)

plot(dta$regime, dta$val)
abline(model)

On Tue, Nov 11, 2014 at 10:39 AM, Iara Lacher <illa...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
Hi All,

I have a question regarding analysis of a unique data set. In simple terms, the data set consists of biomass measures taken in response to several watering regimes. Each watering regime exists for the same length of time, but one regime specifies more water than another.
 
I want to model a regression line through these regimes without simply assigning dummy variables 1 through 3 for each watering treatment. In other words, to perform a regression using true measures of water. Each of the biomass data points are a result of each ENTIRE regime, because death occurs once and that is when biomass is collected.

Do any of you know if there is a way to do this or must I treat each regime as "high", "medium", and "low", i.e. assign dummy variables?

messages.author: befc31f30774e5bc
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Data grouping question
parts:
Hi, thanks for responding!
So, what you did is through 3 regimes that have values representing y values (response measures). The x variable is using each regime 1,2,or 3.
The data I have has values within each of those regimes. So, for example x=1=time series of {8.6,7.5, 6.8, 5.2, 4.9, 3.2, 2.1, 1.0}. x=1 still should be considered as one regime to be compared to regime 2, and regime 3. The y values (responses) cannot be regressed upon the x1 values, for example, because of the way the data was collected (at the end of the time series), but they should be regressed upon x1, x2, and x3.

I don't see how this would be possible, but I am entertaining the thought of a reviewers response (that is probably based on him misunderstanding my methods).  I simply assigned dummy variables for x1, x2... etc. and regressed through that - more like a simple regression (although not quite that simple).

If you have thought, by all means. :)

messages.author: f8f554f3c8aec296
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Data grouping question
parts:
From what I can tell, there's another variable, biomass, that's supposed to be responsive to the watering (val in Erica's simulation). An lm of biomass ~ val would give the dummy variable approach Iara referred to.

To use the actual values of water applied, you can run a mixed model with random effects on the intercept. This way you can predict a common response to the actual values of water applied, but allow for random treatment effects on the intercept.

For example:

dta$biomass <- 5 * dta$val #random linear coefficient for the sake of demonstrating 

library(lme4)
model <- lmer(biomass ~ val + (1|regime), dta)

messages.author: f8f554f3c8aec296
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Data grouping question
parts:
OK thanks for clearing up my confusion.  Since you can't relate individual biomass (y) observations to actual water applied (x) then my suggestion as originally conceived won't work, obviously. Erica's suggestion seems to be what you did (dummy vars for regimes). 

Some info that might help us offer more ideas:

- statement of your overall question
- mockup data set (maybe based off Erica's?) and more detail on the experimental design 
- some details on the reviewer comment could help us comment on that too. 

FWIW here's my understanding so far:

- watering regimes are specified x1, x2, x3
- water is applied at several time points t1, t2, ..tn, over a season, mean amount of water is based on regime but actual amount applied varies
- biomass is harvested at season end
- I'm assuming the goal is to estimate a biologically meaningful parameter 

Some thoughts: 
- if you have some blocking, you could regress block biomass to mean applied water (averaging over times t1..tn) per block 
- even without blocking you could use the actual mean applied water  as the predictor variable, then your coefficient would still have meaningful units. Ideally you would also deal with the errors-in-variables aspect of using the means. Example ignoring that aspect is below.
- estimate a block-level random effect too if you have blocking

## assuming no blocking and ignoring errors in variables issue
dta <- data.frame(regime=c(rep(1,10),rep(2,10),rep(3,10)))
regime.means <- c(8, 4, 2) # hypothetical means for the regimes
actual.water <-    sapply(regime.means, function(x) rnorm(5,x)) # water at times t1..t5 in each regime
dta$water <- c(sapply(colMeans(actual.water), function(x) rep(x,10))) #mean water over times t1 .. t5 in each regime
dta$biomass <-200 + 3 * dta$water + rnorm(dta$water) # a linear response to actual water applied, plus noise, for the sake of argument
str(dta)

lm(biomass ~ water, dta)

## note that fitting this way shouldn't change any anova type comparison 


On Tue, Nov 25, 2014 at 11:40 AM, Iara Lacher <illa...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:
Ok, nope, this isn't it either.

The thing is, the treatment data is a time series... it's the result of the entire *process* of each treatment, not the effect of different values grouped within each treatment.

So, as a hypothetical example: for treatment 1, you start out at 9, go to 8 in a week, to 7 the next, etc. and maybe end at 2. The response of the plant is dependent on the effect of that process, not 9, 8, 7, etc.

That's what I was trying to describe in the figure I sent out.

Does this make better sense?

Iara
